title: DeSlopifying Animations Take 2: implementing your feedback!
author: Ok-Pirate5732
selftext:
I made a post here a few days ago about trying to deslopify the animations in my game and there were a lot of very helpful (and some mean lol) comments pointing out why I did not make as much progress as I thought I was. 

Most of the feedback was about the skating of character movement and the weightlessness of the attacks. The skating I was aware of but just kind of brushed off as something that happens in games, but the weightlessness I was fairly blind to. 

Here is my attempt to fix those! Still a **work in progress** of course, but thought I'd share because the last round was very constructive for me. What I changed: 

* more mechanisms to match player movement with animations and lock feet
* knock back animations with back steps instead of just sliding enemies 
* directional camera shakes
* wind up slow downs and accelerated swings
* hit stops (still need to mess with this a bit, some of the faster weapons appear too glitchy) 
* more exaggerated blood/directional sprays 

Any additional feedback (or if you wanna tell me it still looks like shit lol) welcome of course, thank you!!

*If you're curious, the game is* [*100 Bodies in the Grass*](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5357660/100_Bodies_in_the_Grass/)*, a Hero wave defense set in Vietnam during the time of the 3rd Mongol Invasion*

replies.author: notlemars
replies.body:
It takes a couple days, maybe weeks to figure out “how” to solve these things as a novice. But once figured out, it probably only takes a day maximum to implement a move. 

There’s a running comment out there that “ai is only good in the hands of professionals” and I was completely against it. But after a few weeks of trial and error I realized there are some rules and standards that a professional would understand already that
 a novice like myself needed time to learn. 

Just ranting, because like op, I had a major skating and impact issue in my game. It took a month and a half from the start date to discover a solution, but now that I get it, it takes only a day to make something completely new and polished. A full day though.

replies.author: Ok-Pirate5732
replies.body:
Thank you! Engine is Godot, and mostly using Claude over Astra. Meshy as a start for 3d assets/textures, then anything complex cleaning it up in blender. 

One easy tip for people with little/no experience like me: When I was first messing around with Claude/Godot I was asking "Do X" or "I want Y". Once I started asking "what are the best practices or techniques for achieving X in Godot", and using that as a starting point, it's gotten a lot better and I'm actually learning a lot more this way

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Having a good ruleset for ai helps a lot. You can just ask ai for it but in general you want: 
Less then 300 lines of code per file
Header with the contents for each file
And then if you want to work with multiple agents ( I deploy between 2-12 agents at a time, depending on the workload and what my CPU can handle. 
For multiple agents you need some extra rules for checking in and out of files and inter agent communications. 

Just to name a few

comments.author: thygrrr
comments.body:
This looks very impressive - but the screen shake hurts it! It feels very samey and spiky, like sampling random() - that has infinite frequency.

Pro(mpt)tip: For screen shake, add to a constantly decaying "trauma" value from [0..1] clamped. Continuously sample perlin noise with a nice frequency over time and multiply it by trauma x trauma x constant_amplitude, which becomes your camera "shake offset" (so you get fully differentiable, scalable screen shake that can add up but doesn't completely explode when there's several impacts going on at once).
